# 02. Agreement with the RTB Rent Calculator

**Date:** 8 September 2026
**Sprint:** 2
**Generated by:** `packages/rules/tests/agreement-report.test.ts`
**Summary data:** `data/vectors/agreement-summary.json`

The headline number for the project, plus a finding that changed the product design.

---

## 1. Method

The official calculation runs client side, so rather than probing it as a black box it was
transcribed into a **reference oracle** at `packages/rules/tests/rtb-oracle.ts`, following
`docs/measurements/01` step for step. The oracle is deliberately independent of the engine:
different code, different data structures, and it keeps the RTB's float arithmetic where
the engine uses integer cent.

Source of truth for the transcription:

```
https://rtb.ie/wp-content/themes/rtb/assets/rent-calc/Scripts/rent-calc.js
sha256 1f7a50b86efaba3197232cce6a3d8f86b3f08a651d3a8e6673b6bf83b01432d7
retrieved 6 September 2026
```

The sweep is 10 previous-setting dates x 17 day offsets x 8 rent amounts x the new-build
flag. Dates were chosen to straddle 1 March 2026, to sit either side of the December 2025
to January 2026 CPI fall, and to run past the end of the published table so the
publication-lag fallback is exercised. Offsets cluster around month boundaries so the
`if (day_b < day_a) months -= 1` branch is hit from both sides. Rents include 1 cent,
amounts that are awkward in binary floating point, and 9,999.99.

**2,720 cases compared.**

## 2. The headline result

**The engine agrees with the RTB algorithm on 2,720 of 2,720 cases, exactly, to the cent.**
Both on the maximum new rent and on the maximum increase, which is the figure the official
tool actually displays.

## 3. Why that number is not vacuous

A test that compares two things and always agrees might be measuring nothing. So the same
comparison runs a control: the engine's **statutory** basis, which differs from the RTB by
construction, goes through the identical pipeline.

| | Disagreements with the RTB |
|---|---|
| Engine, RTB basis (the headline) | **0** of 2,720 |
| Engine, statutory basis (the control) | **1,484** of 2,720, 54.6% |

The harness detects differences when they exist. That is what makes the zero meaningful,
and there is a test asserting the control stays non-zero so this cannot rot into a vacuous
comparison later.

## 4. The finding that changed the design

I expected the two readings of section 19(4) to differ by rounding. They do not.

| Gap between the statutory reading and the RTB | Cents | Euro per month |
|---|---|---|
| Median | 405 | 4.05 |
| p90 | 2,872 | 28.72 |
| p99 | 16,438 | 164.38 |
| Maximum | 17,336 | **173.36** |

Only **62 of 1,484** differing cases are within 5 cent. And the gap runs **both ways**:
854 cases where the statutory reading permits more, **630 cases where it permits less**.

That second number is the important one. In 630 of 2,720 cases the official RTB calculator
permits a higher rent than a strict reading of section 19(4) allows. A landlord following
the RTB's own tool correctly would, on this reading, be over the statutory cap.

### The worst case, and why

```
Rent last set  2026-03-01 at 9,999.99
New setting    2026-05-29, new-build exempt so only the CPI cap applies
RTB        previous CPI 105.9 (March), current 106.3 (May)  ->  10,037.76
Statutory  previous CPI 104.2 (Feb),   current 106.4 (April) ->  10,211.12
```

Both differences bite at once. The previous setting is on 1 March 2026, so the statute takes
the month *before* it while the RTB takes the month *of* it, and CPI jumped 1.7 points from
February to March 2026. The one month shift on a large rent is 173.36 euro a month.

The divergence is largest exactly where the law changed, because that is where the index
moved sharply and where the asymmetry in the definition of "previous CPI number" starts to
apply.

## 5. What this changes

**ADR-0006 said "the difference is usually cents" and "the interface should not turn cents
into alarm". That was wrong, and it was wrong because it generalised from one worked
example.** The ADR has been corrected rather than quietly edited.

The decision itself stands: follow the RTB, because that is the number the landlord's
notice will carry and a tenant arguing against the RTB's own calculator needs to know that
is what they are doing. But the consequences change:

1. The second figure is **not** a footnote. Where the gap is material the interface has to
   show it plainly.
2. Where the statutory reading is **lower** than the RTB's, the tenant may have a real
   argument that the increase exceeds the statutory cap even though the landlord used the
   official tool. That is worth telling them, carefully, with the caveat that they are
   arguing against the regulator's own calculator.
3. The size of the gap should be reported in euro per month, not as a percentage, because
   that is the unit the person cares about.

These become Sprint 4 interface requirements.

## 6. Coverage

Enough of the sweep hits each interesting branch that the result is not an artefact of
testing one path:

| Branch | Cases |
|---|---|
| Percentage cap binding | 936 |
| Index cap binding | 1,784 |
| CPI publication-lag fallback used | 1,040 |
| New-build exempt (CPI only) | 1,360 |
| Zero lawful increase | 1,068 |

## 7. The oracle is faithful, checked against the RTB's own code

Everything above rests on the transcription being accurate, and a transcription I checked
myself is not evidence. So rather than typing cases into the form by hand, the RTB's actual
`rent-calc.js` is executed and compared against the oracle directly.

`scripts/verify_oracle.mjs` downloads the live script, runs it under jsdom against a minimal
form carrying the element ids the real page uses, feeds it the same pinned CPI snapshot the
engine uses, and drives its submit handler over a 2,240 case grid.

```
$ node scripts/verify_oracle.mjs
Fetching https://rtb.ie/wp-content/themes/rtb/assets/rent-calc/Scripts/rent-calc.js
sha256 1f7a50b86efaba3197232cce6a3d8f86b3f08a651d3a8e6673b6bf83b01432d7

Compared 2240 cases against the live script.
The oracle reproduces the RTB calculator exactly.
```

The hash matches the file the transcription was made from, so this is a comparison against
the same code, not a later revision. The script reports loudly when the hash changes.

It is a script rather than a CI test on purpose: it needs the network, and it executes the
RTB's copyrighted code, which is fine to fetch and run locally but is not vendored into
this MIT repository.

### The first run failed, and the failure was mine

161 of 2,240 cases mismatched initially. Every one was a case where the oracle returned no
increase and the RTB returned a real one, and all of them had the new-build flag set.

The cause was not the transcription. The case dump was using the trimmed 22 month test
fixture while the script fed the RTB the full 357 month snapshot. The fixture has gaps in
2024, so the oracle's CPI walk-back landed on a month the RTB's never would, and the
comparison was measuring a difference in **inputs** rather than in algorithms.

Fixed by having both sides read the same snapshot from disk. Worth recording because it is
the failure mode this kind of harness is most prone to: two implementations agreeing or
disagreeing for reasons that have nothing to do with either implementation.

## 8. What has not been done

**The three remaining competitor calculators** (righttenantry.ie, propdesk.ie,
tenantsync.ie) have still not been reviewed properly. Carried to Sprint 3.

**Nothing has been typed into the live form by a human.** The jsdom harness runs the real
code, which is stronger than manual entry for coverage, but it does not prove the page
wires that code to the form the way I assume. One manual spot check would close that, and
it is worth doing before the site launches.
